title: Muddy water
hookLine: who can make muddy water clear? let it be still (Tao Te Ching 15)

lines: A SHAKEN JAR OF CREEK WATER.
cards: A jar of creek water, shaken up. Brown, cloudy, you can't see your fingers through it. How do you make it clear?
Stir it faster? Strain it? Fish out the dirt with a spoon?

Each of those keeps the cloud going. The only thing that works feels like doing nothing: set the jar on the counter and leave it alone. Come back later, and the mud lies at the bottom with clear water above it.
Chapter fifteen of the Tao Te Ching asks about exactly that jar.

teach.h: THE MASTERS OF OLD, HARD TO KNOW.
teach.b: First, who the chapter describes: the skilled masters of old, so deep they were hard to know.

So it describes them from the outside, in pictures: careful, like someone crossing a stream in winter; watchful, like someone wary of the neighbors; reserved, like a guest; loosening, like ice about to melt.
And, at the end of the list, murky, like muddy water. Second, the surprise. The masters themselves are compared to muddy water, not crystal, not pure.
Some readers hear humility here: the wise don't look wise; they look ordinary, a little unclear, and don't mind.

teach.h: LET IT BE STILL, AND IT CLEARS.
teach.b: Third, the question, in James Legge's translation: "Who can (make) the muddy water (clear)? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear." The answer isn't a technique. It's stillness and time.
You can't hurry a settling; every effort to speed it up stirs the jar again.
Fourth, a stirred-up mind. After an argument, bad news, a day of too much, the mind is the shaken jar, and the urge is to fix it right now. Sometimes that's needed.
But the chapter points another way: sit, and let the mud find the bottom on its own. Those who hold to this way, it closes, don't want to be full. Room is left for the water to clear.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching use chapter fifteen's image when sitting quietly: instead of trying to clear the mind, they keep still and let the stirred-up thoughts settle on their own.

o: a sign that a spring has gone bad for good
dirty water that must be strained to drink
a stirred-up mind that clears when left still

p: like crossing a stream in winter

s: chapter fifteen says the old masters were as clear as crystal
the list ends: murky, like muddy water. the wise looked ordinary.
the chapter's answer to muddy water is stillness
let it be still, and it will gradually become clear.
the chapter says the wise want to be full
it closes by saying those who hold this way don't want to be full.

games.q: you're holding a jar of shaken, muddy creek water and you want it clear. what do you do?
o: stir it faster to break up the mud.
fish the dirt out with a spoon.
set it down and leave it still.
games.why: "let it be still, and it will gradually become clear." every effort to hurry it stirs the jar again.

practice: Sit and let the body stop moving, and notice whatever is stirred up in you right now: a worry, a plan, the last conversation.
Don't strain it or fish anything out; just watch it swirl, the way you'd watch the jar on the counter, for as long as settling takes. You're not making the water clear, only not shaking it.

wordCard.voice: Muddy water. Chapter fifteen's jar: you can't stir it clear, but let it be still, and it clears on its own. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: muddy, turbid. The water in chapter fifteen, and the word used for the old masters too.

carryVoice: Your line: let it settle. Stillness and time do what stirring can't. Back tomorrow, same hill.
